label: Motivation and mood
rationale: Your energy and mood: no motivation, getting yourself going, perking up, getting hyped, stress piling up.
mixUps: yaruki and genki both 'come out' (deru): yaruki denai is can't get going, genki deta is it gave me a lift, and genki dashite is what you say to someone else. Mood goes up (tenshon agaru) while stress piles up (tamaru); tenshon means hype, not tension.

targets.english: have no motivation, can't be bothered
targets.verbSense: nai: there isn't, have none (negative of aru)
targets.use: About yourself it's the flat 'I just don't feel like it': kyou yaruki nai (I just don't feel like doing anything today). About someone else it's a criticism, they're not trying: ano hito yaruki nai yo ne. In polite talk people usually say yaruki nai desu or yaruki ga nai n desu; yaruki ga arimasen sounds stiff.
targets.notes: yaruki denai is 'I can't get going'; yaruki nai is flatter: I just don't feel like it, or, about others, they don't care.

example.romaji: kyou maji yaruki nai. nanimo shitakunai.
example.ja: 今日マジやる気ない。何もしたくない。
example.english: I've got zero motivation today. I don't want to do anything.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanka yaruki nai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はなんかやる気ないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I just don't feel like doing anything today.

targets.trap: Learners look for an adjective for 'motivated', but everyday Japanese has none. The will to do it 'comes out' (deru): yaruki ga denai. yaruki ga aru (be keen) and mochibeeshon ga agaru are also fine.
partners: chikara (strength: chikara ga denai, can't muster the strength)
targets.use: Mostly said in the negative about yourself, about a task or a day you can't face: yaruki denai (I can't get going). yaruki nai (no motivation at all) is a flatter state and is also said about other people. yaruki aru means keen or motivated; asked as yaruki aru no?, it's a reproach: are you even trying?
targets.notes: yaruki is literally 'do-feeling', from yaru + ki.

example.ja: 今日全然やる気出ない。
example.english: I can't get motivated at all today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa zenzen yaruki ga demasen.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は全然やる気が出ません。
examplePolite.english: I just can't get motivated today.

targets.verbSense: come out, appear; here energy wells up in you
targets.trap: English 'cheer up' is both 'I cheered up' and 'cheer up!', but Japanese splits it: genki deta about yourself, genki dashite to someone else. genki dete! isn't a request, though genki dete kita (I'm perking up) is fine.
targets.use: Mostly past, about what gave you a lift, with ga often dropped: amai mono tabetara genki deta, or arigatou, genki deta after a kind word. The negative genki denai means you can't shake a low mood.
targets.notes: genki moratta (it gave me a boost) is a common way to credit a song, a person or a message.

example.ja: ありがとう、なんか元気出た。

examplePolite.romaji: arigatou gozaimasu. okage de genki ga demashita.
examplePolite.ja: ありがとうございます。おかげで元気が出ました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you. That cheered me up.

targets.politeJa: テンションが上がります
targets.trap: For 'I'm excited', learners say koufun shiteru, which sounds worked-up and, in some contexts, sexual. Say tenshon agaru for hyped right now, and tanoshimi or wakuwaku suru for a plan. False friend: tenshon is energy or mood, not tension.
targets.use: For being hyped right now: tenshon agaru! or tenshon agatte kita. The opposite is tenshon sagaru (get bummed out), and tenshon takai means hyper. It's an informal word: fine with friends and coworkers, but not in formal speech.
targets.notes: English 'tension' or 'nervousness' is kinchou (kinchou suru, get nervous).

example.ja: やばい、テンション上がってきた！
example.english: Oh man, I'm getting so hyped!

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu ne, tenshon ga agatte kimashita!
examplePolite.ja: いいですね、テンションが上がってきました！
examplePolite.english: This is great, I'm getting excited!

targets.politeJa: ストレスが溜まります
targets.trap: For 'I'm stressed', learners turn 'stress' into a verb: sutoresu shiteru, which isn't Japanese. Stress piles up: sutoresu tamatteru. sutoresu o kanjiru (feel stress) and shigoto ga sutoresu (work stresses me out) are also fine.
targets.use: Usually in -te ru for how you are now: sutoresu tamatteru (I'm stressed out). Getting rid of it is sutoresu kaishou, and blowing off steam is sutoresu hassan: karaoke de sutoresu hassan shita.
targets.notes: The transitive is tameru, as in okane o tameru: sutoresu tamenai you ni ne (don't let the stress build up).

example.ja: 最近ストレス溜まってる。
example.english: Stress has been piling up lately.

examplePolite.ja: 最近ストレスが溜まってます。
examplePolite.english: Stress has been piling up lately.

reviewPool.english: sound comes out (of a TV, speaker, phone)
